summary: Technical deep dive focused on structured-output (JSON mode) and tool/function calling performance. Discussed constrained decoding overhead, strategies to minimize latency (prefix/KV cache, batching, quantization), tradeoffs between hosted and Dedicated/private deployments, and security considerations for VPC/on-prem deployments. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share benchmarks and run targeted perf tests; customer to supply security docs and sample workload for pilot.
topics: Function/tool calling latency and RPC overhead
KV cache warm vs cold start behavior
Batching strategies and tail latency impact
Quantization impact on structured output correctness
Validation/parsing strategies for strict JSON outputs
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Martinez: hey everyone, thanks for joining. we scheduled an hour to dig into json mode and function calling perf. quick intros?
[00:12] Rachel Kim: rachel here, head of ml at fincore. we're evaluating options for putting decimal-transcription and trade-recon features behind a low-latency endpoint. main concerns: deterministic structured output and sub-200ms tail for certain flows.
[00:25] Liam Chen: liam from redwood, se on serving. i'll drive the perf parts. fast note — i'll reference some benchmark sheets after the call.
[00:32] Markus Vogel: markus, infra. interested in vpc and on-prem constraints.
[00:38] Priya Singh: priya, security. SOC2 and KMS are top of mind.
[00:42] Sofia Martinez: great. agenda — quick architecture, then constrained decoding in json mode, kv cache and batching, quantization impact, and deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs private).
[01:05] Liam Chen: okay jumping in — when we talk about json mode or constrained decoding, there are two main cost/latency contributors: the model-side decoding cost (additional constraints, beam or grammar enforcement) and the post-processing/validation loop if you run iterative repair. constrained decoding adds per-token overhead because we prune logits and sometimes run an extra check at each step. so in our runtime we optimized the constraint checker to be incremental which reduces the cost, but you'll still see a delta versus free-form decoding.
[01:45] Rachel Kim: when you say incremental, do you mean streaming constraint application? like you check partial JSON grammar as tokens arrive?
[01:52] Liam Chen: exactly. we maintain a tiny state machine for the JSON grammar so we rarely have to re-score the whole beam. that cuts the overhead from ~18% down to ~6-8% on typical models. numbers will vary by seq length.
[02:10] Markus Vogel: is that per-token CPU or GPU? where's the bottleneck?
[02:15] Liam Chen: mostly CPU for the constraint logic, GPU still handles the logits. but because it's per-token and interactive, the round-trip between GPU and the host matters. if you have high inter-op latency on your nodes, it becomes visible in the 95/99.
[02:29] Priya Singh: does that inter-op require any extra surface for secure enclaves or KMS calls?
[02:34] Arjun Patel: (interject) no, KMS calls are orthogonal — encryption/decryption on model artifacts is at load time. runtime inference doesn't call KMS per request unless you do request-level key wrapping which customers usually avoid for perf.
[02:45] Sofia Martinez: good callout. now tool-calling: function calls add both a model planning pass and often an extra RPC when we invoke the external tool. for internal tool-calling (e.g., built-in structured functions), the added tokens for function signature and parsing are the main overhead. for external RPCs it's network + execution time.
[03:10] Rachel Kim: from our side we want the model to return clean json to avoid post-parsing retries. how reliable is json mode? we've seen hallucinated keys previously.
[03:20] Liam Chen: reliability is tied to temperature + constraints + eval prompts. in our tests with deterministic decoding (temperature 0 plus constrained grammar), the structural correctness hits high 90s for short payloads. but content-level hallucination still needs evals. also quantization can increase token-level errors in corner cases.
[03:40] Markus Vogel: let's dig into quantization — we're considering int8/4-bit for cost. what do you observe for structured outputs?
[03:48] Liam Chen: we run model-specific quant profiles. with int8 (symmetrical) we see negligible structure regression for most opt and llm-family models. with 4-bit aggressive quant the noise increases — you may see comma placement or quote errors that break strict json parsers. our runtime has a post-decode fast validator and an optional auto-repair pass that tries minimal edits. but note repair adds latency.
[04:20] Rachel Kim: if repair adds latency, can we do a hybrid: return best-effort json quickly, and then server-side validate and, if fails, do a second fast repair asynchronously, while the primary endpoint returns a warning?
[04:33] Liam Chen: yes, that's a common pattern. we can annotate responses with a sanity flag. for critical flows you can block until validated; for lower priority, you can stream best-effort and trigger a background repair.
[04:46] Priya Singh: background repair — is that processed in the same tenant space? any data residency / logging implications?
[04:52] Arjun Patel: by default yes it's within the same tenant capacity. logs go to your telemetry if you enable it. for private deployments you can disable background repairs or route them to a different cluster to maintain strict isolation.
[05:05] Sofia Martinez: switching to kv cache behavior — two parts: prefix caching (request-level) and full KV for autoregressive generation. the warm cache dramatically reduces latencies for repeated prefixes (like system or function signatures). cold starts are the painful bit.
[05:20] Liam Chen: we see warm cache p50 drop by ~30-40% for common prompts since KV avoids recomputation of past keys. but cold start—if no prefix cached—has to compute the full attention for the prefix and fills the kv which costs. for high concurrency you should size your dedicated pool to keep hot contexts resident.
[05:40] Markus Vogel: what about eviction? memory constraints on GPUs mean we can't keep infinite contexts.
[05:46] Liam Chen: we use an LRU with size heuristics. for Dedicated we let customers set a pin list for critical prefixes so they never evict. on hosted we do heuristics based on traffic.
[05:58] Rachel Kim: about batching — we can't batch some low-latency calls. any suggestions?
[06:04] Liam Chen: yes, batching improves throughput but hurts tail latency. we offer two modes: latency-first (small batches, immediate dispatch) and throughput-first (aggressive batching with slightly higher median). you can also use dynamic batching: small default batch with opportunistic coalescing when queue length grows. that gets you most of the throughput without blowing 99th.
[06:25] Arjun Patel: and our runtime supports continuum batching across sequence positions so short sequences can be packed with long ones efficiently. it's not perfect but it's helpful.
[06:33] Priya Singh: curious about JSON mode + batching. does constrained decoding break efficient batching?
[06:38] Liam Chen: it does complicate things because constraint state is per-request. we vectorize the heavy neural ops still, but the constraint checker runs individually on CPU threads. net effect: GPU ops batched, CPU overhead scales with batch size. there's a sweet spot we measure per workload.
[06:56] Sofia Martinez: let's talk numbers — liam do you have a representative benchmark?
[07:00] Liam Chen: yes quick ballpark from our internal tests with a 13B model on an A100-class node: free-form non-structured median token-latency ~6ms, constrained json-mode token-latency ~8ms (so ~30% token overhead), end-to-end short-payload (20-50 tokens) median ~70ms for free-form vs ~95ms for constrained; 99th jumps more if cold KV. with Dedicated pinned prefixes + warm KV we get short-payload 99th ~120ms in json mode. these are illustrative — we'll share the sheet.
[07:34] Rachel Kim: those token numbers are useful. our SLA target is 200ms 99th for critical flows — seems achievable if we pin prefixes and maybe go dedicated.
[07:42] Markus Vogel: what's the difference between hosted and Dedicated on network path? we need <5ms intra-region if possible.
[07:48] Liam Chen: hosted has multi-tenant network path and may route via a control plane; Dedicated offers colocated instances in your VPC or private endpoint, cutting network hops. for strict low latency we recommend Dedicated in your cloud region or Private deployment on-prem.
[08:05] Priya Singh: for Private/on-prem we need KMS integration and HSM. any known perf tradeoffs?
[08:11] Arjun Patel: HSM/KMS at load-time is fine. if you do request-level crypto (rare) you pay crypto costs. Network wise, running on-prem removes inter-region network variance but you need to size the GPU pool for KV heat.
[08:23] Sofia Martinez: one common ask — can we avoid constrained decoding entirely and instead have the model output JSON as plaintext and run a strongly-typed parser with repair? benefits: simpler runtime maybe faster; downsides: more post-processing retries.
[08:36] Liam Chen: that's valid. we've seen two patterns: strict-constrain-first for critical deterministic endpoints; or heuristic-with-repair for faster median latency. we can help you pick per-route.
[08:49] Rachel Kim: for our transaction-extractors i'd prefer deterministic first for compliance. we can accept slightly higher median if 99th stays under 200ms.
[08:58] Liam Chen: then Dedicated + pin prefixes + int8 quant profile (not aggressive 4-bit) + latency-first batching looks like a sensible starting point.
[09:07] Markus Vogel: curious about tooling around function-calling: do you include the function signature in the tokenization? that seems to bloat the prefix.
[09:15] Liam Chen: yes signatures are part of the prompt; we recommend compact signatures and server-side schemas to avoid giant prefixes. we also support schema references (short id) instead of full JSON schema in the prompt to save tokens; the runtime resolves schema server-side for validation.
[09:34] Priya Singh: any mitigation for tool RPC slowness? some of our tools are internal microservices with 40-120ms latency.
[09:40] Liam Chen: we suggest async tool execution where possible: model returns an intent + payload, you acknowledge and process off-band; or you can pre-warm lightweight functions in the same network fabric. for sync requirements, colocating tool runners in same VPC or using RPC caching helps.
[09:58] Rachel Kim: minor but important — do you emit structured metadata about confidence or token-level logits so we can heuristically detect bad outputs?
[10:05] Liam Chen: yes we can expose per-token logits and a calibrated confidence score, though heavy telemetry has cost and privacy implications. in Dedicated you can enable full token traces.
[10:18] Sofia Martinez: clients sometimes worry about log retention. priya any specific constraints?
[10:22] Priya Singh: we can't retain PII beyond X days and need redaction controls.
[10:26] Arjun Patel: we've got configurable retention policies and on-prem you control logs entirely. we also support redaction hooks before logs hit long-term storage.
[10:35] 
[10:40] (Discussion continues — mid-call demo of sample workload and shared sheet)
[30:12] Liam Chen: demo note: we uploaded a sample workload (short transcripts with fields we expect) to the shared benchmark: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/fin-core-json — you can see raw logs, warm vs cold KV runs, and quant profiles.
[30:29] Rachel Kim: scanning the sheet, i see a case where 4-bit caused a missing comma; that broke our parser in one run. seems intermittent.
[30:36] Liam Chen: yep that's the 4-bit edge case i mentioned. for critical flows we avoid it.
[35:02] Markus Vogel: on the network side, if we do Dedicated in our VPC, how's peering set up?
[35:10] Arjun Patel: typical pattern is private endpoint + VPC peering or Transit Gateway; we provide terraform modules. egress rules are customizable.
[35:22] Priya Singh: if we go private, can we still use Redwood console for observability or is it local only?
[35:28] Liam Chen: both options — we can ship telemetry to your console or to Redwood cloud depending on compliance. in private mode we support local-only observability with a console appliance.
[36:00] Sofia Martinez: ok wrapping up — quick recap of decisions and next steps.
[36:08] Rachel Kim: agreed plan: pilot on Dedicated with pinned prefixes, int8 quant, latency-first batching. we'll supply a 48-hour sample corpus and security questionnaire.
[36:20] Sofia Martinez: action items — listed in the notes. we'll share the benchmark sheet and a proposed pilot timeline.
[36:27] Liam Chen: i'll run additional Dedicated perf tests with your corpus after we get it.
[36:32] Priya Singh: i'll share SOC2 docs and KMS requirements.
[36:36] Markus Vogel: i'll validate network peering details and get back with egress rules.
[36:40] Sofia Martinez: great — thanks all. we'll follow up via email and slack. end.
